title: People supposedly work harder simply because they know they are being watched.
description:
People supposedly work harder simply because they know they are being watched. That lesson comes from a 1920s factory study. There is a problem: the economists who finally found the original data were not convinced it happened as taught.

Coined the term 'Hawthorne effect', nearly three decades after the studies it describes had ended. The name was applied retrospectively to results nobody had cleanly explained at the time.

Output rose in the room where nothing changed too. Researchers dimmed and brightened the lights in one room while leaving a second, unlit control room alone. Productivity climbed in both, which meant the lighting was never the real variable.

How long the original 1924 lighting data sat unexamined, until economists Steven Levitt and John List found it on microfilm in 2011 and reported only weak support for the effect nearly everyone had been taught.

'A glorified anecdote.' Richard Nisbett's verdict on the whole idea: 'Once you have got the anecdote, you can throw away the data.'

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne_effect: read in full. Established the illumination study (1924 to 1927, productivity rose in both the lit experimental room and the unchanged control room), that John R. P. French coined the term 'Hawthorne effect' in 1953, that economists Steven Levitt and John List located the original illumination data on microfilm at the University of Wisconsin in Milwaukee in 2011 and published a reanalysis finding only slight, not drastic, evidence for the effect, that this matched an earlier 1992 reanalysis by S. R. G. Jones, and Richard Nisbett's quoted description of the effect as 'a glorified anecdote'.
- https://www.library.hbs.edu/hc/hawthorne/intro.html: Harvard Business School Baker Library Historical Collections, read in full. Established that Elton Mayo and Fritz Roethlisberger led the study, that it ran nine years (1924 to 1933) at the Hawthorne Works, the manufacturing plant of Western Electric outside Chicago, from the institution's own archival record of the experiments.
